title: Love: not formal when faith is precise; essential when faith means faith working through love
source_text: XCV. Similiter dubitatur, An amor sit actus fidei formalis & essentialis? Affirmant viri doctissimi Chamierus, Wendelinus, Wittichius & Cocceius; alii vero negant. Quantum ad me attinet, puto hic esse aliqua distinctione opus. Fides enim potest duplici modo sumi. Primo praecise, secundum id quod habet a spe, charitate, ac reliquis Christianis virtutibus distinctum. Hoc sensu amor non est fidei actus formalis; sed ad aliam virtutem, nempe charitatem pertinet. Secundo fides sumitur, pro aggregato quodam plurium actuum sive habituum, qui comprehenduntur sub nomine fidei per charitatem operantis. Et ita, plerique Reformati notant se fidem sumere in hac quaestione, nempe, non pro uno actu vel habitu simplici, sed pro complexu plurium actuum vel habituum. Unde est quod illam locant non in solo intellectu, sed etiam in voluntate, quia complectitur actus, tum ab intellectu, tum a voluntate elicitos, & habitus facultatem utramque informantes. Ut videre est apud Chamierum, Wendelinum, Paraeum, & alios, ubi de subjecto fidei disputant. Ad fidem autem prout comprehendit omnes actus, quos complecti solemus sub nomine fidei per charitatem operantis, proculdubio pertinet, tanquam actus ei essentialis, amor Dei Christique sincerus, sine quo fides viva & per dilectionem operans concipi non potest.
pass_a_gloss: Likewise it is doubted whether love is a formal and essential act of faith. Most learned men affirm — Chamier, Wendelin, Wittich, and Cocceius; but others deny. As for me, I think some distinction is needed here. For faith can be taken in a twofold way. First precisely, according to that which it has distinct from hope, charity, and the remaining Christian virtues. In this sense love is not a formal act of faith; but pertains to another virtue, namely charity. Second, faith is taken for a certain aggregate of many acts or habits which are comprehended under the name of faith working through charity. And so most of the Reformed note that they take faith in this question not for one simple act or habit, but for a complex of many acts or habits. Whence it is that they locate it not in the intellect alone, but also in the will, because it embraces acts elicited both from the intellect and from the will, and habits informing both faculties. As is to be seen in Chamier, Wendelin, Paraeus, and others, where they dispute of the subject of faith. But to faith as it comprehends all the acts which we are accustomed to embrace under the name of faith working through charity, without doubt there pertains, as an act essential to it, sincere love of God and of Christ, without which living faith working through love cannot be conceived.
pass_b_english: Is love a formal essential act of faith? Chamier, Wendelin, Wittich, Cocceius say yes; others no.
Le Blanc distinguishes: take faith precisely (apart from hope and charity) → love belongs to charity, not as faith’s formal act.

Take faith as the aggregate “faith working through love” (how most Reformed take it here) → intellect and will together; sincere love of God and Christ is essential — living faith cannot be conceived without it.

lemmas.gloss: to be taken in a twofold way
sincere love of God and of Christ

choices.term: Hoc sensu amor non est fidei actus formalis
choices.english: In this sense love is not a formal act of faith
choices.why: Precise sense separates charity from faith’s formal act.
rejected: Love is never essential under any sense of faith
